newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Base metals head south for summer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Base metals head south for summer.

text.p: Industrial metals remained under pressure on Tuesday as investors reduced their exposure to the sector ahead of the traditionally slow summer quarter in the Northern Hemisphere.
Not even a strike at the western world's biggest nickel producer could stem the flow of money out of the London Metal Exchange base metals' futures markets.
"The metals, in general, now look vulnerable to further spates of selling pressure," broker Rudolf Wolff said in a daily market report.
An early rally in several metals in a knee-jerk response to news of a strike at Canadian nickel/copper producer Inco Ltd was short-lived as investors hungrily sold into the higher levels.

This soon turned prices lower, a trend which was aided by Russia's biggest nickel/copper producer, Norilsk, forecasting its 1997 output of the metals would rise by 20 percent and nine percent respectively.
"According to our plan...the Norilsk Nickel group proposes by the end of this year to hit 213,000 tonnes of nickel, 370,000 tonnes of copper..." group spokesman Sergei Vetchinin said.
The feeling among metal traders was that the Inco strike would not begin to impact on nickel prices unless it became clear that a long stoppage was in prospect.
"Nickel stocks are currently on a rising trend with Russian producers shipping to Europe and this would cushion the market from a strike, provided it was not prolonged," a trader said.
By the end of the day the three months delivery copper prices had fallen to $2,479, having been above $2,500 earlier.
Aluminium traders reported an easing in recent tight supply pipelines and this contributed to an $18 fall to a six week low of $1,578 a tonne.
Nickel, after rallying $300 in early trade, fell back to settle at $7,180 at the end of the day.

Among other commodities coffee remained volatile although swings were not as wild as the past two days. At the day the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) July coffee futures were up $40 a tonne at $2,150.

Traders said that roasters appeared to have covered their most urgent needs and could possibly sit back and not chase the market so hard but they did not see prices giving up too much ground while the Brazilian crop was under threat from frost during June and July.

Investment funds were noted taking an interest in the LIFFE white sugar futures contract which offered the prospect of tighter supplies in the summer months when the market suffers from a tailing off in old crop EU supplies and the start of the new crop availability in September/October.
In the precious metals gold traded tightly around the $344 an ounce level but platinum and palladium shot higher despite the likelihood of Russia resuming exports this month.
"The market is still very tight in the near term...you've still got to pay up for metal," a trader said.
Platinum was up about $15 at $415/$419 an ounce and
palladium rose $22.50 to $193/$197.
